lines.note: Rusu wo moru means staying to guard the house. The scan supplies the omitted paragraph mark and caſa, not eaſa. The first vowel of Ruſuuo is badly abraded; the surviving stroke is compatible with u, and the house-watching context supports this chosen reading rather than the misleading kana hint for Riſu.
Yama wo moru gives the second example of guarding or watching, here a mountain or wooded area. The printed paragraph mark was omitted by OCR.
Monte, ou mato completes the preceding object: the mountain or woodland. This short continuation remains a separate physical line.
Morin is explained by shigeru hayashi, a dense wood. The Portuguese reads Boſque, not Beſque. The written-register label S. is upright in the scan, separately from the italic gloss.
Mǒrio is explained as midarini omonbakaru, thinking rashly or wrongly. Ruins begins the Portuguese description of bad thoughts, continued below; the caron is retained.
Penſamentos, ou conſiderações completes the definition of improper thoughts or considerations. Both nouns belong to Mǒrio above.

The explanation voboro voboro and the weather gloss identify obscurity or haze. The scan nevertheless prints Môuô, with u rather than the expected r of Môrô; this is retained, and the supplied NINJAL index independently flags that printed anomaly (167a03). This completes tẽ-po and describes overcast or misty weather. The written-register label S. belongs to this entry and is set upright, not as part of the italic Portuguese gloss.
Moroashi denotes both feet. The gloss explicitly gives the paired-body-part sense of moro-.
Morobito means all people and is equated with Xonin. P marks poetic usage; the Portuguese homẽs retains its abbreviation tilde.
Morokata means both shoulders. The example is physically divided after Moro-, and its hyphen must not be removed by joining the word.
Katauo nuide completes morokata wo nuide: baring both shoulders. The Portuguese Deſpindo describes undressing or uncovering them.

runs.text: Certo genero de peixe de rio, que ha

lines.note: Moroco is a named kind of freshwater fish. The definition begins a geographical restriction that continues onto the next row, rather than identifying a modern species.

The fish is said to occur in the lake of Omi. The embedded place-name is printed in italic within the Portuguese explanation. The second pass establishes a v-shaped caron over o, correcting OCR Võmi to Vǒmi without modernizing the name.
Morokoshi is equated with Taitǒ and glossed China. The caron on the final o of Taitǒ is clear; the alternative-name separator remains printed i,.
Morokuchi refers here to both sides of a horse's bit. Esquerda, & di- begins the contrast between left and right; the divided Portuguese word continues below.

runs.text: reita do ferro por õde leuão às vezes dous o ca-

lines.note: This completes direita and explains that two people sometimes lead the horse by opposite sides of the bit. The line ends with ca-, whose continuation is on the next row.
Valo completes caualo. Uma no morokuchi wo toru means taking hold of both sides of the horse's bit; the Portuguese rendering begins Leuarẽ, with its final abbreviation mark.
The first gloss finishes the description of two people leading the horse. A new paragraph then begins Morocuchini, continued by its causative verb below.

runs.text: Fazer leuar o caualo desta maneira.

lines.note: Morocuchini ficaſuru means making the horse be led in this manner. The causative form is supported by Fazer leuar; printed historical spelling and spacing are retained.
Moroi describes something fragile or perishable. The example starts Mo- at the right edge and continues as moroi inochi on the following row.

runs.text: Vida breue, ou q̃ logo ſe acaba.

lines.note: Moroi inochi is a frail or short-lived life. The Portuguese explains it as a brief life, or one that soon ends; q̃ is retained unexpanded.

runs.text: Arroz que està feito em vinho antes

lines.note: Moromi is the fermented rice mixture before pressing. The Portuguese speaks of rice already made into wine; its description continues below.
De ſe eſpremer completes the stage description: before the mixture is squeezed or pressed. It belongs to Moromi, not to the next headword.

runs.text: Vinho que eſtà ainda por eſpre-

lines.note: Moromizake names the still-unpressed rice wine. The scan supports eſtà, correcting OCR eſts; the divided infinitive continues below.

runs.text: mer juntamente com o arroz cõuertido ja na ſu-

lines.note: The wine remains together with the rice already converted into its substance. The abbreviation cõuertido is retained, and ſu- is a physical division of ſuſtancia.
This completes ſuſtancia do vinho, the substance of the wine. It is the end of the Moromizaqe definition, not a new entry.
Moromoro means all or the various members of a group. The example Moromorono fi- continues into fito on the next physical row.
To completes fito in the example meaning all people. The Portuguese repeats Todos os homẽs with the printed abbreviation.
Moroqe gives a verb meaning to disintegrate or dissolve. Its principal forms are retained rather than modernized to a present-day conjugation.
The gloss compares disintegration to overcooked fish. The example begins Xôguo, small fish: the capital X and guo are visible, without the OCR's extra r.

The example says that when cooking small fish one does not slit the belly, fearing that the fish will fall apart. The long ſ in ſaqezu, supported by the unsplit-belly sense, corrects OCR faqezu; farauatauo retains f. Moroqẽ carries an abbreviation tilde, not a long-vowel accent.

runs.text: O peixe miudo aßi ſemlhe ti

lines.note: Kotouo voſoru completes the fear that the fish will fall apart. The Portuguese begins the recommendation to cook small fish without removing the guts; its final ti continues as tirar on the following row without a supplied hyphen.

runs.text: rar as tripas he bõ cozelo pera q̃ ſe não desfaça.

lines.note: This completes tirar and explains the purpose: leaving the guts in helps prevent the fish from disintegrating. The scan separates as tripas; the historical bõ and cozelo are retained.

Morote means both hands. The separate right-edge (juntos. is visibly printed on this row but semantically completes Todos in the following Morotomoni entry; it is preserved in its physical position rather than moved into that sentence. No full stop is established after mãos. The entry is flush left, not indented.
Morotomoni means both together, and then all together. The displaced juntos. is physically above at the right of c1-l035; the two rows are not joined or reordered in the diplomatic text.

runs.text: Certo verniz fino que ſe poem por

lines.note: Morourushi is a fine lacquer, described here as a varnish put over another material. The visible v after Moro corrects OCR y and reflects the urushi element; the supplied NINJAL index agrees on the lexical identification (167a17).
The lacquer is applied over the leather of scabbards. This completes the preceding relative clause and does not name another material independently.
Mosaku is paraphrased saguri, motomuru, searching or seeking. The Portuguese verb investigar is divided after in-; its continuation and Buddhist label are below.

This completes investigar, to investigate or search. The weak final vowel is read as a rather than OCR e. The second pass retains the aligned round s in the connected st type; Bup. is a roman Buddhist-domain label, not a Japanese word or a partly italic headword.

The Japanese paraphrase means bringing an accusation rashly or without basis. Enlargement supports Midarini, not Xidarini, and a worn long ſ in Mǒſô rather than t. The printed final circumflex is retained even though the lexical index flags the headword as an apparent misprint for Mǒso (NINJAL 167a19).
This completes falſamente and explains the accusation as unfounded or lightly made. The wording belongs to the accusation entry, not to the following bamboo name.
Mǒſochicu names a Chinese bamboo. The first o bears a caron; the following o is unmarked in this impression, so the expected long vowel in the lexical name is not supplied.
Mǒſot denotes fierce people, such as warriors. The faint initial caron is retained, and the final checked t is not expanded to tçu; the supplied NINJAL index corroborates this headword (167a21).

This names a particular preparation or serving of cooked rice, with iy representing rice. The worn ſ followed by round s corrects OCR is; both o vowels show carons. The printed initial long-vowel marking is retained despite the lexical index's warning about an apparent anomaly (NINJAL 167a22).
The rice is given by the Ienxùs, the Zen religious group named in the Portuguese gloss. This is an embedded Japanese term, not a standalone synonym or a new headword.

runs.text: Certa laya de barretes de que vſão os

lines.note: Môſu names a type of cap. The bottom row is recoverable in the scan despite the severely garbled OCR; its definition continues at the top of column 2 with the wearers and occasions of use.

runs.text: Ienxùs em festas, ou em pubrico.

lines.note: This completes the cap entry from the bottom of column 1: Ienxùs wear it at festivals or in public. The historical printed pubrico is retained rather than silently changed to publico.
Mosuso is the edge or hem of a garment. The Portuguese vestido and the two long-s sorts in Moſuſo are retained as printed.
Motague gives the verb for raising or lifting. Its feet example begins A- at the right edge; the following row supplies the remainder of ashi.
Ashiuo motaguru means raising one's feet. The Portuguese specifies lifting them oneself, and the row completes the example begun above.

runs.text: Hum vaſo de vinho, como boyão.

lines.note: Motai denotes a wine vessel, compared with a large jar or pot. Boyão is the historical Portuguese container word as printed.
Môtan and Môtô are alternative forms for something extremely small or slight. The separator l means or; all three marked o vowels here have circumflexes.
Motaxe means a present or gift. The example begins the honorific form vomo-taxeno, physically divided across two rows.
The example refers to seeing the things just received as the recipient's gift. The printed continuous monodomouo and mimaraxite are retained; the citation label and translation follow below.

runs.text: Vendo ainda agora voſſo preſente, ou

lines.note: Mon. is the citation label for the gift example. The translation begins with seeing the addressee's present just now; it is not a fresh Japanese headword.
This completes the description of the gift as the things the addressee sent. The visible stop after couſas is retained even though it interrupts the syntax.
Motaye means to last or remain alive. Its principal forms are followed by a separate example about the continuation of life.
Inochiuo motayuru means continuing to live. The Portuguese Durar cõ vida confirms this sense and preserves the abbreviation mark over o.
Motçure means becoming tangled or caught. The second Portuguese infinitive is physically divided as trauar / ſe, without an added line-end hyphen.

runs.text: ſe algũa couſa com outro. Vt,

lines.note: The gloss describes one thing entangling with another. Yuqu michi begins the example's path along which the subject travels.
Vines have grown thick along the path and catch the traveller's feet. The doubled zz in cazzuraga and tt in xiguette are retained as printed.

runs.text: Emburulharſe a era nos pees que estaua eſpeſſa

lines.note: The Portuguese renders the vegetation as era, ivy, tangled around the feet. This historical spelling is kept rather than supplied with modern h; the description of its dense growth continues below.

runs.text: no caminho. ¶ Itẽ, Ser embaraçado, & pou-

lines.note: The first sentence completes the path example. A second sense is then introduced: being hindered or slow in business; embaraçado is one printed word, correcting the OCR's internal space.
This completes pouco expedito nos negocios. A further Japanese example begins Fana nadoni mo-, but the scan does not establish a terminal hyphen, so none is supplied.

runs.text: Não ſe poder apartar de ver as

lines.note: Tçururu completes motçururu: being caught or absorbed in such things as flowers. The Portuguese explains an inability to turn away from looking.
The object of that prolonged attention is flowers or another such thing. This closes the figurative entanglement sense.
Mote aſobi means taking pleasure or recreation. The printed space within the headword and the circumflex in the past-form abbreviation ôda are retained.
Tçuqi fanauo mote aſobu gives the example of enjoying the moon and flowers. Recrear is continued by ſe on the next physical row, without an inserted hyphen.

runs.text: ſe com ver a lũa, & roſas, ou flores.

lines.note: The Portuguese completes the recreation example as viewing the moon, roses or flowers. The scan supports final a in lũa and o in flores, correcting OCR lũs and fleres; the visible mark over u is retained rather than normalized away.

runs.text: Couſa cõ q̃ hũ folga, ou ſe

lines.note: Moteasobimono is an object with which one amuses oneself. The headword begins Mote-, not the OCR's Mute-; the Portuguese reflexive verb continues below.
Recrea completes the definition of an object used for amusement. The row is short but is a genuine continuation of Moteaſobimono.
Moteatçucai means handling or treating someone or something. Both principal-form endings have carons; Saiaino begins a cited example concerning an only child.
The example says that the child was the parents' only child and that they would not let the child tread even on dust. Fumaxe- is continued by ji on the next row.

runs.text: ji, araqi cajenimo atejito motte atçucai,

lines.note: The protective treatment extends to not exposing the child to a rough wind. The printed spelling motte atçucai, including doubled tt and the word space, is retained.

runs.text: Lib. 29. Sedo filho dãtre ambos. ſ.

lines.note: Tai is the citation label, followed by book 29. The Portuguese begins by calling the child the offspring of both parents; its final ſ. is the explanatory abbreviation, not a hyphenated word.

runs.text: de marido, & molher, o tratauão de maneira q̃

lines.note: The gloss identifies the two parents as husband and wife and introduces how they treated the child. Molher and the abbreviated q̃ retain the historical spelling.

runs.text: nẽ tocaße cõ os pès ẽ terra, nẽ o vẽto lhe deße,

lines.note: The parents prevented the child's feet from touching the ground and the wind from striking the child. The scan separates pès ẽ; the grave accent and abbreviation tilde are kept separately.

runs.text: ou fizeſſe nojo. ¶ Itẽ, Enfadarſe, ou canſar

lines.note: The wind was not to cause discomfort. A new paragraph introduces the further sense of becoming tired or annoyed through prolonged handling of something.

runs.text: de tratar muito algũa couſa Vt,

lines.note: The additional sense is weariness from dealing with something too much. Cono cotouo begins the example, and no separate stop is established between couſa and Vt in the scan.
The example means being already tired of this matter. The scan separates Eſtou ja, correcting the OCR's joined form; the past-form o has a caron.
Motefayaxi means esteeming or favouring someone. The historical principal forms in ſu and aita are retained, and fauore- continues below.
The example begins with a person who has no merit or accomplishments. The continuation links this concessive clause to others' praise or favour.
Praising or favouring that person makes the person appear to have merit. The scan retains a word space in mote fayaxeba and a caron in aruyǒni.

runs.text: Poſto que ſeja homem ſem partes, &

lines.note: Mon. is again a citation label. The Portuguese begins the concession that the man has no qualities or accomplishments, continuing the same example.

Habilidades completes the lack of accomplishments; the initial is h, not OCR b. The scan prints the unusual fouore- and a terminal hyphen, so the vowel is retained while the OCR's final dot is corrected.

runs.text: cendoo faz parecer que as tem.

lines.note: Cendoo completes the divided verb for favouring him. The gloss concludes that such treatment makes him seem to possess the qualities he lacks.
Motenaxi is the verb for receiving or entertaining someone hospitably. The visible ſu is retained in the principal forms rather than following a differently edited index form.
The definition illustrates hospitality by inviting someone. It completes the verb entry, before the separate noun below.
The noun Motenaxi denotes hospitality or good treatment. It is a distinct printed entry despite sharing its form with the preceding verb stem.
Môtô, equated with Caxxiqi, denotes boys living at religious establishments in preparation for becoming Buddhist monks. Both headword accents are circumflexes.

runs.text: relas pera ſerem Bonzos, & perſinal trazem

lines.note: The boys are there to become Bonzos, and a visible sign distinguishes them. The historical continuous perſinal is retained rather than modernized to por sinal.

runs.text: de pendurado ſobre a testa alguns cabelinhos

lines.note: Their distinguishing sign is a few hairs left hanging over the forehead. Enlargement supports cabelinhos through the worn middle letters, correcting the OCR's cabelmnhos; the sentence finishes below.
The hair is retained before the boys are shaved. This closes the entry; the material below it is page furniture, not another body line.
